message_to_team: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy remain one of the leading causes of maternal death in the UK. The MBRRACE-UK 2025 report found that 83% of women who died from hypertensive disorders could have had better care — a striking reminder that outcomes in this condition are not inevitable. This month we revisit the evidence: what NICE NG133 actually says at the bedside, and whether the drugs we reach for postpartum are truly backed by data.

ctg_meeting.title: The Baseline That Was Telling Us Something
ctg_meeting.background: Patient on IOL with propess in situ. Initial CTG baseline 120 bpm at 03:30; risen to 140 bpm by 10:30 with possible reduced variability — no action taken, documentation form not completed.
ctg_meeting.interpretation: At consultant ward round (15:00): baseline 160 bpm, definitely reduced variability, chemoreceptor decelerations — decompensating CTG. Propess removed, terbutaline given, transferred to delivery suite with some delay.
ctg_meeting.outcome: Baby delivered in theatre; APGAR 9 and 10, mild-to-moderate cord gas acidaemia. Flagged as near-miss.
ctg_meeting.learning_point: A 10% rise in baseline is a red flag. The failure here was delayed escalation and normalcy bias, not lack of recognition. Dr Shu Wong proposed adding a baseline comparison field to the antenatal CTG documentation form.
ctg_meeting.trace_caption: Figure 1. CTG trace demonstrating a decompensating pattern on induction of labour: baseline tachycardia at 160 bpm, markedly reduced variability, and chemoreceptor decelerations — prompting emergency transfer to the delivery suite.

guidelines.title: NICE NG133: Hypertension in Pregnancy — Diagnosis and Management

sections.label: Definitions
sections.text: Chronic hypertension (booking or <20 weeks), gestational hypertension (≥20 weeks, no proteinuria), pre-eclampsia (hypertension + proteinuria, organ dysfunction, or placental dysfunction). Avoid 'essential hypertension' until secondary causes excluded.

sections.label: Prevention & targets
sections.text: Aspirin 150mg from 12–36 weeks if one high-risk or two moderate-risk factors. Treat if BP >140/90; severe threshold >160/110. Target: 135/85.

sections.label: Antihypertensives
sections.text: Antenatal: labetalol → nifedipine → methyldopa (nifedipine first-line in Afro-Caribbean women). Postnatal: enalapril first-choice with renal monitoring at one week; nifedipine/amlodipine preferred in Black and Caribbean women.

sections.label: Admission & delivery
sections.text: Deliver at 37 weeks; within 24–48 hours if diagnosed after 37 weeks. Admit for BP >160/110, creatinine >90, ALT >70, platelets <150, worsening bloods, impending eclampsia, or foetal compromise.

sections.label: Postnatal & long-term
sections.text: GP review at 6–8 weeks; check proteinuria resolved. Pre-eclampsia carries ~1-in-6 recurrence risk and 3x lifetime cardiovascular risk. Prescribe antihypertensives at 05:00/11:00/17:00/23:00 to enable post-dose BP monitoring and support earlier discharge.

journal_club.title: Nifedipine vs Enalapril for Postpartum Hypertension: Does the Evidence Support the Switch?
journal_club.key_findings: Open-label RCT of 94 women with gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, or chronic hypertension randomised to enalapril (10–40mg daily) vs nifedipine (30–90mg daily). Primary outcome: composite healthcare burden index.
journal_club.key_results: Only a 2% difference in primary outcome (NNT 45) — well below the 30% the trial was powered to detect. Severely underpowered, prone to type 2 error, and affected by provider and participant bias. Enalapril was not superior, though safe in breastfeeding and associated with lower diastolic BP at six weeks. Ethnicity was not reported — a notable gap given NICE guidance on antihypertensive choice in women of Black or Caribbean background.
journal_club.take_home: Evidence does not support switching from nifedipine to enalapril postpartum. Antihypertensive choice should factor in ethnicity, side effect profile, and dosing convenience.

ai_in_clinical_practice.title: Using AI Better: Four Prompting Habits for Everyday Clinical Work

key_points.label: Set up custom instructions
key_points.detail: Tell ChatGPT who you are so responses are calibrated to your level.

key_points.label: Specify your audience
key_points.detail: Framing the prompt around who the answer is for produces vastly different outputs.

key_points.label: Show, don't describe
key_points.detail: Upload an existing trust document as a template for style-matched outputs.

key_points.label: Use study mode
key_points.detail: Type /study at the start of a chat for interactive, test-as-you-go teaching.

ai_in_clinical_practice.safety_reminders: Never share patient-identifiable data. Always verify clinical content against guidelines. Microsoft Copilot is available free via the trust.

historical_fact.title: The Urine That Changed Everything — Guy's Hospital, 1843
historical_fact.fact: In 1843, John C. W. Lever at Guy's Hospital tested the urine of 10 women with puerperal convulsions and found albumin in 9 — the exception dying of meningitis. Eclampsia was considered purely neurological at the time. Lever proposed it differed from Bright's disease because the albuminuria resolved after delivery — the first time a systemic, detectable precursor to eclamptic convulsions had been identified, and the intellectual ancestor of the dipstick dipped at every antenatal appointment today.
